data.line1: The land holds its breath before the shutter opens.
data.line2: We scroll past the image and save it for later. Later rarely comes. The light doesn't wait, and neither does the threshold. You are there for it, or you are not.

data.body:
The Infinite Arch started as a trail name. A play on my last name and the idea that every arch leads to a path worth discovering. It became a brand because it became a belief. What's next? The next trail, the next race, the next adventure with friends and family. I started hiking and running later than most people would expect, and I have not stopped since. Every arch opens onto another path. Every path leads somewhere I have not been yet. A name, a brand, and a reminder that the possibilities are infinite if you keep moving forward.
I came to photography the same way I came to the trail. Slowly, and later than most people would admit. Life moves fast, and I wasn't good at stopping to see the world around me. The camera fixed that. I shoot Fujifilm GFX medium format and X Series digital. I still load film into a vintage Minolta X-700, because film asks something digital does not. It asks you to commit. Every frame costs something. Every shutter press is a decision.
The paths I have chosen have taken me to the summit of Guadalupe Peak, at 8,751 feet the highest point in Texas. To the black volcanic sand of Reynisfjara, and into the crevasses of Vatnajökull, Europe's largest glacier. And back down the forgotten back roads of North Texas, where the land is flat and the sky goes on forever. These are the journeys that go beyond the daydream.

data.body: Randy Archambault is a fine art photographer based in Frisco, Texas. Shooting under The Infinite Arch, he works with Fujifilm medium format and vintage film cameras across landscapes, journeys, and the moments most people scroll past. His work explores passage, presence, and what waits on the other side of the daydream.
data.heading: Artist Bio

data.body:
The tools are few and chosen carefully.

For medium format digital work, two Fujifilm GFX bodies: the GFX 100S II and the GFX 100RF. The former for deliberate, considered shooting; the latter for work that asks for something more compact, more present in the landscape. Both render with a quality of light that still surprises, even after years of use.

For lighter expeditions and moments that call for speed over deliberation, the Fujifilm X-E5. Small enough to disappear into a jacket pocket, capable enough to hold its own against far larger systems.

Then film. A Konica Hexar RF, a Minolta X-700, a Yashica Electro 35. Each with its own character, its own way of slowing the act of seeing. Film cameras ask something different of the photographer: a certain commitment, a willingness to trust the frame before it is confirmed. That tension is part of what makes them worth carrying.

The gear is not the point. But the right tools, used honestly, tend to stay out of the way and let the work happen.

data.body:
The Infinite Arch takes its name from two things at once: the natural arch in rock and the arch of a human life. Both describe the same passage: a threshold between what was and what's possible.

I shoot Fujifilm's GFX medium format system because 102 megapixels demands intention. Every frame is a choice. Every trip into the field is a commitment to be present for whatever the light decides to do.

This work is landscape as contemplation. The camera is the last step in a process that begins with arriving, waiting, and being willing to return. The image is the record of that patience.

portfolioWorks.description:
Some things refuse to disappear. A dam holding back a river that no longer needs holding. A church standing at the edge of a plain where the congregation long ago scattered. A sign whose letters have faded past legibility but whose iron post still drives into the caliche like an act of faith. These are not ruins, exactly. Ruins imply defeat. What I find instead are presences, structures that have outlasted their purpose and arrived at something quieter and more durable than use.

I come to them with the GFX, or sometimes the X-E5 when the road narrows and the light demands speed, and I try to photograph not what they were but what they have become. Witnesses. That is the word that keeps returning. They stood before I arrived and they will stand after I leave, holding their vigil over landscapes that have no other memory. The land forgets. Stone and steel and old timber do not, or at least they forget more slowly, carrying the weight of the people and the weather and the particular quality of silence that accumulates in a place no one visits anymore.

Iceland offered its own version of this. So did Guadalupe Peak, and the Chihuahuan desert stretching south toward nothing. Different geologies, different climates, the same essential fact: something was built here, and the building outlasted the builders, and now it keeps watch.

portfolioWorks.description:
There is something that shifts when a figure enters the frame. The landscape doesn't diminish — it clarifies. Scale arrives, and with it, something closer to truth.

These photographs follow people moving through open country: Zoë walking toward a horizon that keeps its distance, strangers crossing a bridge without knowing they're being watched, figures small against terrain that was never as empty as it appeared. Each one carries the quiet suggestion that we have always gone to wild places in search of something we struggle to name at home.

What interests me isn't the solitude of wilderness but its companionship — the particular intimacy of shared passage, the way a journey changes when you make it alongside someone else, or simply not alone. These are the people encountered on the way through: some known, some not, all of them briefly part of the same unfolding distance.

portfolioWorks.description:
The far places. The ones that ask something of you before they offer anything back. Iceland's volcanic interior, where the ground still remembers its own making. The long Appalachian light that arrives sideways and stays just long enough to change what you thought you understood. The Oregon coast where the continent simply runs out, and the Pacific receives that fact without comment.

Each journey here was a deliberate act — not of escape, but of arrival. Going somewhere in order to become still. To wait for the light to do what you had quietly suspected it might, if you were patient enough and present enough to deserve it. The suspicion, it turns out, is the practice. You carry it across time zones and weather systems and return home unsure whether you succeeded, until the contact sheet tells you otherwise.

This is where film earns its place. The Hexar loaded, the frame finite, the decision irreversible. No reviewing, no adjusting, no undoing. Just the moment accepted or missed, and the discipline of not always knowing which.

These images gather the Iceland 2026 expedition alongside other journeys that refused to be understood from a distance: Alaska's scale that humbles without requiring spectacle, the particular and unhurried quiet of rural Québec, the compressed and layered world of Japan encountered slowly, on foot, in weather that kept changing its mind. Five geographies, one disposition. Elsewhere, in the end, is not a place you reach but a way of paying attention — practiced repeatedly, imperfectly, and without guarantee of arrival.

portfolioWorks.title: Becoming
portfolioWorks.subtitle: Choosing the next version of yourself.
portfolioWorks.description:
The autobiographical thread runs through everything here. Starting over, later than most, and moving forward anyway. Hiking, running, photography — all of it taken up deliberately, as a way of deciding who to become next. Not as escape, but as authorship.

The arch isn't the subject. It never was. What interests me is the perspective that only comes from passing through something, the way the frame changes what you see on the other side. This is the chapter about walking through it. About choosing motion over stillness, becoming over having been. The images in this series are less about arrival than about the quality of attention that sustained movement makes possible.

Later than most. And moving forward anyway.
